name: Annie Besant
role: British reformer and Indian National Congress president (1917)
summary: Besant campaigned for women’s political rights and organized with workers in Britain, where she wrote in favor of Fabian socialism. After embracing Theosophy she promoted religious education and campaigned for Indian self-government.

sacred-nation.rationale: Besant described a nation as a portion of divine life that unites successive generations and gives its people a distinctive role in the world.

legalize-sex-work.rationale: Besant denounced prostitution in her marriage pamphlet. No position on whether consensual adult sex work should be a criminal offense was found.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Besant established the Central Hindu College to teach Indian religion and culture alongside Western subjects and to reverse the estrangement from Indian traditions she attributed to colonial education.

nation-first.rationale: Besant argued that Indian participation in a federation would serve both India and wider interests and called for the combined strength of free nations to be used in the service of the world.

basic-income.rationale: Besant’s communal system shared output with workers, children and people incapacitated by age or sickness, and withheld support from an able-bodied adult who refused work.

state-directs-investment.rationale: The Case for India: she hopes the Government help given to munition factories in war will continue to industrial factories in peace, and blames the bureaucracy's laissez-faire for foreign takeover of India's mineral and dye industries.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Besant praised the constitutional Crown as a common head for a voluntary union of free nations and urged that the autocratic imperial title in India be dropped.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Besant rejected treating ancient revelations as binding on society and argued that many scriptural injunctions should be set aside as unsuitable for present conditions.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Besant argued that a stable constitution should start from social obligations and drew on the Indian ideal of mutual duties instead of treating society as a balance of individual rights.

limit-population.rationale: Besant published and promoted practical means of limiting family size, then after becoming a Theosophist stopped reprinting her own pamphlet and refused to sell its copyright because she no longer endorsed teaching the method.

distribute-by-need.rationale: Besant described a social order in which members contribute according to capacity and receive social support according to need.

profit-exploitation.rationale: Autobiography, her 1884-85 socialist writings object to huge fortunes accumulated out of the toil of others; she does not state the full claim about profit from owning businesses.

individual-rights-only.rationale: Besant attributed the right of self-rule and self-development to both individuals and nations, and treated the freedom of nations as a collective right in her argument for federation.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Besant argued that revelations must ultimately be judged by reason and praised sacred texts for the moral truths that readers could verify.

work-for-welfare.rationale: Besant argued that an able-bodied adult offered productive employment by the community should receive no relief if they refused it.

class-collaboration.rationale: The Changing World (1909): liberty will never come 'by hatred of class against class'; she wants co-operation and profit-sharing and says the great change must come from above, not below. Her 1880s Autobiography stressed union of all workers against idlers, so +1.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Besant’s Indian constitutional plan assigned ward councils responsibility for schools, sanitation and food inspection in addition to ordinary public order.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: Besant praised Indian states that made religious instruction part of public schooling and urged education in the religion of each pupil’s parents.

reviewHistory.rationale: The Changing World (1909): 'in our education we must have religious teaching, in order that we may have a firm foundation for morals', on a broad basis common to the faiths. This is her later, Theosophical position; as a Secularist and on the 1888 School Board platform she stood for secular education, so this reverses her earlier view.

constituent-assembly.rationale: Besant wanted India to frame its own constitution through conventions composed of elected council members with power to co-opt additional participants.

collective-defense.rationale: Besant argued that every member of the Indo-British Commonwealth should come to the defense of any member attacked from outside, citing India’s wartime support for Britain.

moral-incentives.rationale: Besant called for self-sacrificing service in her theosophical lectures. The record does not establish that she wanted social duty to replace material rewards as the main incentive for work.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: The Case for India: 'Other-Government emasculates a Nation, lowers its character, and lessens its capacity'; Britons must give up the idea that India is a possession and treat her as an equal self-governing partner.

animal-use-humane.rationale: Besant’s vegetarian argument called for abstaining from food that required an animal to be killed, including where killing was distinct from other forms of cruelty.

reviewHistory.rationale: Vegetarianism in the Light of Theosophy: she argues for abstaining from all animal food that implies slaying the animal, and holds that meat-eating degrades the slaughterers and is a moral responsibility on the eater. She does not discuss humane slaughter separately.

institutions-fit-civilization.rationale: Besant argued in The Future of Indian Politics that imposing Britain’s political constitution on India disregarded the distinct history, traditions and social arrangements on which Indian institutions needed to build.

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: The Future of Indian Politics: she broke with Gandhi in 1919 over passive resistance because breaking other, non-tyrannous laws seemed illogical and absurd and would breed lawlessness; she wrote articles on the sanctity of law.

punish-blasphemy.rationale: Besant condemned the use of blasphemy laws to punish disbelief and challenged the distinction they drew between free criticism of Christianity and legally protected doctrine.

reviewHistory.rationale: The Christian Creed (1883) attacks the blasphemy laws as persecution by bigots against free speech, and in her defence before the court in the Autobiography she calls them bad laws unfairly revived.

participatory-democracy.rationale: Besant proposed elected village and ward councils and public discussion, but no clear general position on direct public participation in decisions beyond representative institutions was found.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: In her mature theosophical lectures Besant praised publicly run schools that taught children their parents’ religion and called for that approach to become the model for national education.

shared-marital-authority.rationale: In her marriage pamphlet Besant denounced a husband’s legal authority over his wife and proposed a written partnership between spouses with mutually specified rights and duties.

reviewHistory.rationale: Marriage pamphlet: marriage should be a contract between equals and not a bond between master and servant, with marital control ceasing to exist and a wife holding the same property rights as if unmarried.

income-for-work-not-ownership.rationale: Besant argued that workers should receive the full product of their labor and proposed distributing the surplus of communal industries among their workers instead of paying it to owners.

culture-before-state.rationale: Besant built institutions for Indian religious and cultural education to restore national confidence and train Indians for self-government before pursuing Home Rule through her newspapers and the Home Rule League.

scripture-inerrant.rationale: Besant held that purported revelations contain contradictions, interpolations and immoral teachings and must be assessed by reason.

no-business-privileges.rationale: Besant opposed fiscal arrangements under which British legislators would favor British businesses, citing favoritism by colonial authorities as a burden on Indian merchants and manufacturers.

tech-with-ancestral-values.rationale: Besant proposed combining the application of modern science in agriculture, industry and education with institutions grounded in India’s historical traditions, and presented Eastern religion and Western applied science as complementary.

humans-entitled-to-use-animals.rationale: Same vegetarianism lecture and her condemnation of vivisection in The Changing World; she rejects both animal food and animal experiments, so she does not hold the entitlement as stated.

pay-for-effort.rationale: Besant argued for an equal share of communal surplus across occupations. She did not address whether pay should vary with individual effort.

one-spouse-at-a-time.rationale: Marriage pamphlet: loyalty of one man to one woman is the highest sexual ideal and monogamy is the result of civilization. She states it as an ideal, not as a legal prohibition, so +1.

opposition-only-legal-channels.rationale: Besant opposed a specific civil disobedience campaign under colonial rule and chose constitutional methods for Home Rule. No categorical rule about all opposition under repression was found.

arbitrator-settles-disputes.rationale: Besant proposed replacing war with international arbitration and wanted a federation working through the League of Nations to make that alternative effective.

reviewHistory.rationale: The Changing World: working to substitute arbitration for war is 'a great deal more practical' than nursing the wounded; she does not discuss whether arbitration should bind.

free-basic-services-for-all.rationale: Besant’s Commonwealth proposal made elementary education free. The materials did not establish a right to all basic public services free of charge.

civil-marriage.rationale: Marriage pamphlet: she proposes a simple public declaration, a written contract of partnership that should be stamped and registered when the law permits, in place of the present legal forms.

decent-living-guarantee.rationale: Autobiography, her 1884-85 Socialist writings: 'health, comfort, leisure, culture, plenty for every individual', 'enough for each of work, of leisure, of joy'. Stated as a social ideal, not as a guarantee by the state, so +1.

notes: Research covered the Fabian essay on industry and municipal government, the birth-limitation campaign and later reversal, marriage and the franchise, theosophical education and ethics, criminal justice and animal welfare, Indian Home Rule and constitutional design, wartime policy, international arbitration and the proposed Commonwealth. Besant’s religious views changed from secularism to Theosophy. Her mature position is used where she explicitly reconsidered an earlier view, and both phases of her publishing record are used for population limitation.
